text: High-impact work - running, rope, plyometrics, hard spinning - transmits ground reaction force up the kinetic chain into the lumbar spine, which is why a back injury removes those options first.
verified_by: Stated as the general mechanical rationale for low-impact resistance work rather than as a claim about her diagnosis. The University of Exeter release frames the intervention as 'simple resistance exercises' performable at home as an alternative to conventional higher-impact training, and Pvolve's own method description (PR Newswire, 22 Aug 2023) contrasts its approach with 'repetitive stationary motions' on the grounds of joint load. Her own trainer confirms the injury-specific consequence: 'she had a back injury but she can do this workout and not inflame those old injuries' (HELLO!, 2 Feb 2026). No claim is made in the narration about the specific diagnosis, level or severity of her injury.
picture: Spine anatomy diagram; runner foot strike slow motion; force arrow overlay

text: Pvolve is low-impact resistance training using bands, ankle bands, a weighted ball and light weights, trained through three planes of motion rather than one repeated stationary pattern.

text: A 12-week randomised trial at the University of Exeter, led by Professor Francis Stephens, put 72 women aged 40-60 on either four Pvolve sessions a week or the standard 150 minutes of weekly activity. SESSION LENGTH IS DISPUTED BETWEEN THE TWO SOURCES: the University of Exeter release states all classes were 30-35 minutes; Pvolve's own study page states 30-55 minutes. The narration states both figures out loud and tells the viewer to prefer the university's.
verified_by: University of Exeter news release: 72 healthy active women aged 40-60, not on HRT, 12-week intervention, randomised to Pvolve resistance training or standard 150 minutes weekly activity; participants 'committed to joining classes four times a week'. DISCREPANCY, RECORDED DELIBERATELY: the Exeter release reads 'All classes were 30 to 35 minutes in duration', whereas Pvolve's own study page (https://www.pvolve.com/blogs/all/healthy-aging-clinical-study) reads '4 Pvolve workouts per week of 30-55 minutes in length'. Both pages were re-read directly in this pass and the wording above is verbatim from each. The larger figure is the funder's and the smaller is the research institution's; the narration gives both and instructs the viewer to take Exeter's, because W7's whole argument is that the sponsor's framing should not be taken on trust. Conducted at Exeter's Nutritional Physiology Research Unit by Professor Francis Stephens' group.
